exam.title: Statistics - Beginner Exam
exam.subtitle: Fundamentals of Probability and Statistics
exam.instructions: Answer all questions. Show all work and calculations. Permitted aids: Non-programmable calculator, standard normal distribution table. Good luck!

exercises.title: Drawing without replacement
exercises.description:
An urn contains $5$ red, $3$ blue and $2$ green balls. Two balls are drawn without replacement.
a) What is the probability that both are red?
b) What is the probability that the balls have different colours?
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Part a): Path rule
First ball red: $\frac{5}{10}$. Second red given that the first was red: $\frac49$ (only $9$ balls left, $4$ of them red). $P(\text{both red}) = \frac5{10}\cdot\frac49 = \frac{20}{90} = \frac29 \approx 0.222$.

Step 2: Part b): Complement
“Different colours” is the opposite of “same colour”. $P(\text{rr}) = \frac{5\cdot4}{90} = \frac{20}{90}$, $P(\text{bb}) = \frac{3\cdot2}{90} = \frac{6}{90}$, $P(\text{gg}) = \frac{2\cdot1}{90} = \frac{2}{90}$. Sum: $\frac{28}{90}$.

Step 3: Part b): Result
$P(\text{different}) = 1 - \frac{28}{90} = \frac{62}{90} = \frac{31}{45} \approx 0.689$.

Step 4: Check via combinatorics
There are $\binom{10}{2} = 45$ pairs; same colour: $\binom52 + \binom32 + \binom22 = 10 + 3 + 1 = 14$. $P = 1 - \frac{14}{45} = \frac{31}{45}$ ✓. Both ways must agree.

exercises.title: Permutations and combinations
exercises.description:
A class has $12$ students ($7$ boys and $5$ girls).
a) In how many ways can a class representative, deputy and treasurer be chosen?
b) In how many ways can a $4$-person delegation be chosen?
c) What is the probability that a random delegation contains at least one girl?
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Part a): With order
The offices are different, so order matters: $12\cdot11\cdot10 = 1320$ (arrangements without repetition).

Step 2: Part b): Without order
For the delegation the order does not matter: $\binom{12}{4} = \frac{12\cdot11\cdot10\cdot9}{4!} = \frac{11880}{24} = 495$.

Step 3: Part c): Complement
“At least one girl” is the opposite of “only boys”. $\binom74 = 35$ delegations consist only of boys.

Step 4: Part c): Result
$P = 1 - \frac{35}{495} = \frac{460}{495} = \frac{92}{99} \approx 0.929$. Check via decomposition: $\binom51\binom73 + \binom52\binom72 + \binom53\binom71 + \binom54 = 175 + 210 + 70 + 5 = 460$ ✓.

exercises.title: Total probability and Bayes
exercises.description:
Machine $A$ produces $60\,\%$ of the parts ($2\,\%$ defective), machine $B$ $40\,\%$ ($5\,\%$ defective).
a) What is the probability that a random part is defective?
b) A part is defective. With what probability does it come from machine $A$?
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Given quantities
$P(A) = 0.6$, $P(B) = 0.4$, $P(D|A) = 0.02$, $P(D|B) = 0.05$ ($D$: defective).

Step 2: Part a): Law of total probability
$P(D) = P(D|A)P(A) + P(D|B)P(B) = 0.02\cdot0.6 + 0.05\cdot0.4 = 0.012 + 0.020 = 0.032$.

Step 3: Part b): Bayes' theorem
$P(A|D) = \frac{P(D|A)P(A)}{P(D)} = \frac{0.012}{0.032} = 0.375$.

Step 4: Check and interpretation
$P(B|D) = \frac{0.020}{0.032} = 0.625$ and $0.375 + 0.625 = 1$ ✓. Although $A$ produces more parts, $62.5\,\%$ of the defective parts come from $B$ because $B$ has a higher reject rate.

exercises.title: Binomial distribution
exercises.description:
The probability that a student passes an exam is $0.8$. In a group of $10$ students let $X$ be the number of students who pass.
a) Determine $P(X = 8)$.
b) Determine $P(X \geq 9)$.
c) Determine expectation and variance.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Model
$X \sim B(10;\ 0.8)$: $10$ independent trials with success probability $p = 0.8$. $P(X = k) = \binom{10}{k}0.8^k\,0.2^{10-k}$.

Step 4: Part c): Expectation and variance
$E(X) = np = 8$, $\operatorname{Var}(X) = np(1-p) = 10\cdot0.8\cdot0.2 = 1.6$, standard deviation $\sqrt{1.6} \approx 1.265$.

Step 5: Plausibility check
The most likely value is near the expectation $8$: $P(X = 8) \approx 30\,\%$ is indeed the largest single value ($P(X = 9) \approx 27\,\%$, $P(X = 7) \approx 20\,\%$).

exercises.title: Normal distribution
exercises.description:
The height of men is normally distributed with $\mu = 175\ \mathrm{cm}$, $\sigma = 8\ \mathrm{cm}$.
a) Determine $P(170 < X < 180)$.
b) Which height is not exceeded by $90\,\%$ of men?
c) Determine $P(X > 185)$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Standardisation
$Z = \frac{X - \mu}{\sigma} = \frac{X - 175}{8} \sim N(0,1)$.

Step 3: Part b): Quantile
We need $x$ with $\Phi\left(\frac{x - 175}{8}\right) = 0.9$. From the table $z_{0.9} \approx 1.2816$. $x = 175 + 8\cdot1.2816 \approx 185.25\ \mathrm{cm}$.

Step 5: Consistency check
Since $185 < 185.25$, $P(X > 185)$ must be slightly larger than $10\,\%$: $10.6\,\%$ ✓. Rule of thumb: $P(|X - \mu| < \sigma) \approx 68\,\%$; here $170$–$180$ is $\pm0.625\sigma$, hence smaller, $46.8\,\%$ ✓.

exercises.title: Measures of location and spread
exercises.description:
The grades of an exam are: $1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3, 4, 4, 5$.
a) Compute arithmetic mean, median and mode.
b) Compute sample variance and standard deviation.
solutionSteps:
Step 2: Part a): Median and mode
$n = 9$ is odd: the median is the $5$th value of the ordered list, i.e. $3$. Mode (most frequent value): $3$ (occurs three times).

Step 3: Part b): Sum of squared deviations
$\sum(x_i - 3)^2 = 4 + 1 + 1 + 0 + 0 + 0 + 1 + 1 + 4 = 12$.

Step 4: Part b): Variance and standard deviation
Sample variance (division by $n - 1$): $s^2 = \frac{12}{8} = 1.5$, $s = \sqrt{1.5} \approx 1.225$. (Dividing by $n$ would give $\frac{12}{9} \approx 1.33$.)

Step 5: Check
The deviations from the mean sum to $0$: $-2 - 1 - 1 + 0 + 0 + 0 + 1 + 1 + 2 = 0$ ✓. Mean, median and mode agree: symmetric distribution.
